summary: The federal budget passed, Ontario's school unions all hold strike mandates, Stellantis meets Ottawa and Ford today on Brampton, and negotiators say Canada can't wait out Trump.
body: The federal budget passed the House of Commons on Thursday, 162 to 151. It adds billions in new borrowing and tax measures, mostly for infrastructure and building projects, and the Liberals now hold a majority of seats after byelections and floor-crossings.[^1] Measures include a large tax deduction for business investment and a top-up to a benefit for lower-income families. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the borrowing pushes costs onto Canadians, and the NDP says the budget caters to big business.[^2]

In Ontario, all five major education unions now have strike mandates. Results released Thursday show 94.2% of more than 57,000 school support workers voted yes, after teachers' unions voted 96% to 98% in favour.[^3][^4] A mandate is not a strike: the unions say they want negotiated deals, and support staff start bargaining on Nov 30. Education Minister Paul Calandra said the results were not surprising.[^3]

Today, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Premier Doug Ford and Unifor's Lana Payne meet Stellantis about its plan to sell its Brampton plant to defence firm Roshel, which puts about 2,200 auto jobs at risk. CTV's sources say Stellantis expects the sale to go ahead.[^5] Ford says it is Ottawa's job to stop the sale; Joly says Stellantis must do its part.[^5][^6]

On US trade, top negotiators told Carney's advisory committee on Thursday that Canada cannot simply wait out Trump's last two years, and hope for an interim deal on autos, steel and lumber tariffs before Jan 1.[^7] Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro attacked Ottawa online, saying "Canada cheats us".[^8]
differences: On Brampton, Ford blames federal costs and says Ottawa must stop the sale, while Joly says Stellantis must do its part.[^5][^6] On the budget, the government says it invests for growth; the Conservatives and NDP say it borrows too much or favours business.[^2]

reads.title: Canadian negotiators dispel idea Canada can just play for time in trade talks with Trump
reads.summary: Why Canada's negotiators think tariff-hit industries cannot wait for a new US president, and what an interim deal might cover.
